MUQATIL:12:88-90/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:12:88-90/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:12:88-90/r4.claim: God favored Joseph and Benjamin; whoever avoids adultery and bears harm patiently receives the full reward of doing good.

TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r1.claim: Joseph confirms his identity, points out Benjamin, and says God favored them by reuniting them after separation.

TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r2.claim: Piety means performing obligations and avoiding sins; patience means restraining oneself from forbidden speech or action during affliction, for God preserves the reward of the good.

TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r3.claim: Most readers recite the brothers’ words as a question; Ubayy’s reported form is أو أنت يوسف, while Ibn Muhaysin reads it as a statement.

TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r4.claim: Al-Tabari prefers the interrogative reading because the recognized body of reciters unanimously supports it.

TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r5.speaker: ابن إسحاق
TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r5.claim: Ibn Ishaq says the brothers recognized Joseph when he lifted the veil after asking whether they knew what they had done to Joseph and his brother.

TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r6.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v13p327#2/r6.claim: Mujahid glosses piety and patience as avoiding disobedience to God and enduring imprisonment.

ZAJJAJ:v3p128/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p128/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p128/r1.claim: The question has several hamza readings: both fully realized, the second softened between hamza and yāʾ, or an alif separating the two; it may also be read as a declarative ‘you are Joseph.’

ZAJJAJ:v3p128/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p128/r2.speaker: الشاعر
ZAJJAJ:v3p128/r2.claim: An unnamed poetic line ‘are you [the one]’ illustrates the two hamzas meeting.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p351/r1.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p351/r1.speaker: ابن كثير
IBNMUJAHID:v1p351/r1.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads إنك لأنت يوسف as a declarative statement; every other reader uses an interrogative.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p351/r2.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p351/r2.speaker: حمزة والكسائي وعاصم وابن عامر
IBNMUJAHID:v1p351/r2.claim: These readers use two hamzas in أءنك; the others use one.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p351/r3.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p351/r3.speaker: ابن كثير
IBNMUJAHID:v1p351/r3.claim: Ibn Kathīr, in Qunbul's transmission, retains yāʾ in يتق in both liaison and pause; the others omit it in both.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r1.speaker: ثابت البناني
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r1.claim: The sons of Jacob heard of an Egyptian who fed the poor and filled an orphan's lap; they thought he must be from their family and discovered he was Joseph.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r2.speaker: ابن أبي الجلد
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r2.claim: Joseph's brother said Joseph resembled his lost brother, like the sun; Joseph prayed that the God of Jacob would show mercy to his childhood and return his brother.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r3.speaker: ابن اسحاق
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r3.claim: Joseph had not held his brother responsible for what he himself did to separate the brothers, since they had wronged Joseph; his disclosure made them recognize him, and he said God had favored them and that God rewards piety and patience.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r4.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r4.claim: An earlier scripture says envy harms the envier but not the envied; patience saves the envied person, as the verse promises reward to the pious and patient.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r5.speaker: إبراهيم
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2193#2/r5.claim: To fear God and be patient means to avoid fornication and endure celibacy.

NAHHAS:v2p343/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p343/r2.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p343/r2.claim: The second hamza may be lightened, articulated, or separated by alif; in إنه من يتق, hā' refers to the matter.

FARISI-HUJJA:v4p447/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v4p447/r1.speaker: ابن كثير
FARISI-HUJJA:v4p447/r1.claim: Ibn Kathir reads إنك لأنت يوسف as a statement; all others make it a question, supported by Joseph's answer and the reported wording أو أنت يوسف؟ in Ubayy's codex.

FARISI-HUJJA:v4p447/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v4p447/r2.speaker: حمزة والكسائي وعاصم وابن عامر
FARISI-HUJJA:v4p447/r2.claim: They pronounce two hamzas in أإنك; the remaining readers use one, according to their usual rules for two adjacent hamzas.

FARISI-HUJJA:v4p447/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v4p447/r3.speaker: ابن كثير
FARISI-HUJJA:v4p447/r3.claim: Ibn Kathir alone, through Qunbul, retains yāʾ in يتقي in both liaison and pause; the other readers omit it in both contexts.

FARISI-HUJJA:v4p447/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v4p447/r4.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v4p447/r4.claim: The retained yāʾ in ويتقي ويصبر can coordinate on the semantic position of the conditional response; alternatively, its vowel may be omitted for ease, as in other Quranic and poetic forms.

FARISI-HUJJA:v4p449/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v4p449/r1.speaker: أبو الحسن
FARISI-HUJJA:v4p449/r1.claim: Abu al-Hasan reports hearing رسلنا لديهم with a quiescent lām; this supports easing the vowel before فإن الله in the reading ويصبر.

FARISI-HUJJA:v4p449/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v4p449/r2.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v4p449/r2.claim: The vowel may be dropped as in ابن كثير's reading ويتقه; treating تقه like كتف/علم supports the same easing in ويصبر.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p252#2/r1.claim: In a report continuing from the prior excerpt, Jacob's son says he consoled himself with a younger maternal brother; after that brother was taken, Yusuf wept at the brothers' accusation and threat.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r10.speaker: ابن إسحاق
THALABI:v5p252#2/r10.claim: Ibn Ishaq says Yusuf's question uncovered the truth and lifted the veil, allowing the brothers to recognize him.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r11.speaker: الضحاك
THALABI:v5p252#2/r11.claim: A report through al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas says Yusuf's pearl-like teeth when he smiled made the brothers associate him with Yusuf.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r12.speaker: عطاء
THALABI:v5p252#2/r12.claim: A report through Ata from Ibn Abbas says the brothers recognized Yusuf after he removed his crown, revealing a white mark shared by Jacob, Isaac, and Sarah.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r13.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p252#2/r13.claim: Yusuf says God favored the brothers and him by bringing them together after their separation.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r14.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r14.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p252#2/r14.claim: The verse explains piety as fulfilling obligations and avoiding sins, and patience as abstaining from what God forbids.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r15.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r15.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v5p252#2/r15.claim: Ibn Abbas specifies piety as avoiding adultery and patience as remaining celibate.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r16.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r16.speaker: مجاهد
THALABI:v5p252#2/r16.claim: Mujahid says piety means avoiding God's disobedience and patience means enduring prison.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r17.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r17.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p252#2/r17.claim: The brothers admit Yusuf was favored over them in knowledge, judgment, intellect, virtue, beauty, and kingship.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r2.speaker: بعضهم
THALABI:v5p252#2/r2.claim: Another account says Benjamin named three sons Yusuf, Wolf, and Blood so he would remember Joseph; Yusuf choked up, then asked what they had done to Joseph and his brother.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p252#2/r3.claim: One explanation says a sinner is ignorant at the moment of sin, even when acting deliberately.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v5p252#2/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets إذ أنتم جاهلون as meaning they were children.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r5.speaker: الحسن
THALABI:v5p252#2/r5.claim: Al-Hasan interprets the brothers as young men; the author finds this plausible because youth is especially associated with ignorance.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p252#2/r6.claim: The brothers could be blamed for Benjamin's treatment because they accused him over the cup and said Rachel's sons were unlike them.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p252#2/r7.claim: A second explanation is that the brothers mistreated Benjamin after Joseph's loss because the two were from the same mother.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r8.speaker: ابن محصن
THALABI:v5p252#2/r8.claim: Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir read the opening as a statement, إنك, while the other readers use the interrogative.

THALABI:v5p252#2/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p252#2/r9.speaker: أبي بن كعب
THALABI:v5p252#2/r9.claim: Ubayy ibn Ka'b's reading أو أنت يوسف supports the interrogative reading.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r10.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r10.claim: God does not waste the reward of those who do good either in this world or in the next.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r11.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r11.claim: آثرك الله derives from preferring one person over another.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r12.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r12.claim: A cited poem uses آثرك الله to mean that God selected or preferred someone, witnessing the lexical meaning of preference.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r6.speaker: عبد الله
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r6.claim: A reading attributed to Abdullah adds that Joseph and his brother are kin: وهذا أخي وبيني وبينه قربى.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r7.claim: God favored Joseph and his brother first with safety and then with honor; the favor may also be their reunion after long separation.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r8.speaker: إبراهيم
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r8.claim: One interpretation of fearing God and being patient is avoiding fornication and enduring celibacy.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r9.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p74#2/r9.claim: Alternatively, it means fearing God and patiently enduring affliction.

QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r10.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r10.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r10.claim: Joseph accepts the brothers’ correction and speaks from surrender to divine decree, forgiving them without claiming his piety as his own.

QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r6.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r6.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r6.claim: By saying this is my brother rather than calling the others his brothers, Joseph hints that their conduct was not brotherly.

QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r7.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r7.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r7.claim: Mentioning Benjamin softens the shock of Joseph’s revelation, just as God’s question about Moses’ staff occupied him during the divine disclosure.

QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r8.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r8.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r8.claim: Joseph testifies that God does not waste the reward of those who are Godwary and patient.

QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r9.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r9.speaker: أبو علي الدقاق
QUSHAYRI:v2p90/r9.claim: Al-Daqqaq says Joseph initially attributed his reward to his patience, but his brothers corrected him: God’s choice, not his own merit, gave him precedence.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r1.speaker: أكثر القراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r1.claim: Most reciters read أإنك لأنت يوسف as a question; Ubayy's reading is أو أنت يوسف.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r2.speaker: الضحاك
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r2.claim: In Juwair's report from al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās, Joseph asked whether they knew him, smiled, and they recognized his pearl-like teeth and asked if he was Joseph.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r3.claim: The response أنا يوسف supports the interrogative reading because Joseph is answering what they asked.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r4.speaker: ابن كثير
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r4.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads the phrase as a statement; a report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the brothers recognized Joseph only when he removed his crown and they saw his family birthmark.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r5.speaker: ابن إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r5.claim: Ibn Isḥāq says Joseph lifted the veil and his brothers recognized him.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p233/r6.claim: Ibn Kathīr's reading may still be understood as an interrogative with the question particle omitted, though such omission is rare outside poetry.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r1.claim: To fear and be patient means to fear God and endure trials while refraining from sins.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r2.speaker: ابن الأنباري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r2.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī summarizes this as watching God and patiently bearing harm for His sake.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r3.speaker: مقاتل بن سليمان
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r3.claim: Muqātil b. Sulaymān glosses piety as avoiding fornication and patience as enduring harm.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r4.speaker: إبراهيم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r4.claim: Ibrāhīm interprets the traits as avoiding fornication and enduring celibacy.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r5.claim: The reward God does not waste is the reward of whoever has these traits and those who act like them.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r6.speaker: ابن كثير
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r6.claim: In the Qunbul transmission, Ibn Kathīr reads من يتقي with the yāʾ retained.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r7.speaker: أبو علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r7.claim: One analysis deletes the short vowel of the final yāʾ to leave it silent under the jussive; Abū ʿAlī rejects this as a poetic-only feature in ordinary speech.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r8.speaker: أبو علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r8.claim: Alternatively, من is a relative pronoun that does not govern the jussive; the coordination follows its semantic conditional force, allowing ويصبر to be nominative with its vowel omitted.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r9.speaker: ابن الأنباري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234#2/r9.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī offers a third analysis: the yāʾ in يتقي is an added fleeting letter that carries the kasra of the qāf.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r1.speaker: ابن الأنباري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r1.claim: Joseph says his proper name rather than “I am he” to foreground the wrong his brothers did and God's compensation of victory and love; “this is my brother” identifies another wronged and favored person like himself.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r2.claim: Arabs repeat a word or expression to magnify its importance, as in the cited line about nothing preceding death.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r3.claim: “God has favored us” means He granted every good in this world and the next.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r4.claim: Another interpretation is that God favored them by reuniting them after their separation.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p234/r5.claim: The meaning of المنّ was explained at 2:262.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:90-93/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:90-93/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:90-93/r1.claim: Joseph identifies himself to his brothers and says God reunited him with his wronged brother after they had been separated.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:90-93/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:90-93/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:90-93/r2.claim: God does not waste the reward of those who fear him and patiently endure hardship.

JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r2.speaker: أبو جعفر وابن كثير
JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r2.claim: They read the opening hamza of أإنك as kasra, making the phrase declarative in form.

JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r3.speaker: نافع ويعقوب
JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r3.claim: They read أإنك with a short, unlengthened opening hamza; the reading is interrogative.

JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r4.speaker: أبو عمرو
JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r4.claim: He reads the interrogative with a lengthened opening hamza; this form is also Qālūn's report from Nāfiʿ.

JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r5.speaker: ابن عامر وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي
JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r5.claim: They read two hamzas; all the listed forms other than the declarative reading are interrogative.

JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r6.speaker: الزجاج
JISHUMI:v5p3703#2/r6.claim: Arabic permits four treatments of the two hamzas: lighten both, insert an alif between them, soften the second, or use one hamza as a statement.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r1.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو جعفر
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r1.claim: Ibn Kathir and Abu Jafar read إنك as a declarative statement; the other readers make it a question.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r2.speaker: ابن إسحاق
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r2.claim: Ibn Ishaq says Joseph spoke from behind a curtain; after he asked what they had done, the covering was lifted and they recognized him.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r3.speaker: الضحاك عن ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r3.claim: Al-Dahhak, citing Ibn Abbas, says Joseph smiled, and his pearl-like teeth made his brothers suspect he was Joseph.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r4.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r4.claim: Ata, citing Ibn Abbas, says the brothers recognized Joseph by a birthmark near his temple, shared by Jacob, Isaac, and Sarah; another view says they guessed until he confirmed it.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p273#2/r5.claim: “This is my brother” identifies Benjamin, and God’s favor was to reunite the two brothers.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p274/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p274/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p274/r1.claim: To fear God means fulfilling obligations and avoiding sins; patience is refraining from what God forbids.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p274/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p274/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p274/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas explains fearing God as avoiding adultery and patience as enduring celibacy.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p274/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p274/r3.speaker: مجاهد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p274/r3.claim: Mujahid explains fearing God as avoiding sin and patience as enduring prison.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r1.claim: The question a-innaka is read interrogatively or affirmatively; Ubayy's reading adds aw anta Yusuf, with the first alternative elided, conveying repeated astonishment.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r2.claim: They recognized Yusuf from his appearance and manner of speech, or from his pearl-like teeth when he smiled, or a mark shared with Jacob and Sarah.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r3.claim: Yusuf mentions his brother because that detail explains who he is in answer to their question, even though they already knew his brother.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r4.claim: Yattaqi means fear God's punishment, while yasbir means refrain from sins and persist in obedience; muḥsinīn replaces a pronoun because it includes both qualities.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r5.claim: The brothers confess they deliberately sinned, lacked piety and patience, and were humbled while God raised Yusuf through his virtue.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r6.claim: Tharīb means reproach; its root evokes removing the fatty covering of the stomach, a metaphor for stripping dignity by rebuke.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r7.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p473#2/r7.claim: Today may attach to no reproach, to the understood phrase upon you, or to forgiveness; alternatively today God forgives them as a promise of immediate pardon for repentance.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p474/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p474/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p474/r1.claim: At the conquest, Muḥammad asked Quraysh what they expected him to do; after they answered, he said he would speak Joseph's words, No reproach upon you today.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p474/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p474/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p474/r2.claim: When Abu Sufyan came to embrace Islam, al-ʿAbbās told him to recite Joseph's pardon; the Prophet prayed that God forgive him and his teacher.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p474/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p474/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p474/r3.claim: The brothers felt ashamed to accept Joseph's daily hospitality; he said their kinship and descent from Abraham made them honored in Egyptian eyes.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p474/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p474/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p474/r4.claim: Joseph said the Egyptians saw his brothers through their first impression, but their kinship with him and descent from Abraham had raised them in people's eyes.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r4.claim: Readers vary in the interrogative hamzas in أإنك; other forms insert an alif or ease the second hamza.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r5.speaker: ابن محيصن وقتادة وابن كثير
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r5.claim: These readers use the declarative إنك, though some understand it as a question with the interrogative particle omitted.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r6.speaker: أبي بن كعب
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r6.claim: Ubay’s reading asks whether he is Joseph or whether the other brother is Joseph; Abu al-Fatḥ explains an omitted predicate.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r7.speaker: مجاهد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r7.claim: Mujahid interprets piety as avoiding sin and patience as enduring prison.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r8.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r8.claim: Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi reads piety as abstaining from fornication and patience as remaining celibate.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p276#2/r9.claim: The verse intends a general principle covering major trials; the interpreters specify Joseph’s own experiences because those were his circumstances.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p277/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p277/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p277/r1.claim: Most readers omit the final yāʾ in يَتَّق, while Ibn Kathir retains it; several grammatical explanations are offered.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p277/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p277/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p277/r2.claim: One explanation treats the yāʾ as vocalized and the jussive as loss of its vowel, but Abu ʿAli rejects this as a poetic rather than spoken construction.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p277/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p277/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p277/r3.claim: Other explanations make من mean الذي with يتقي indicative and يَصبر coordinated by meaning, or treat يَصبر as raised but with a shortened final vowel.

TABRISI:12:88-93/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:88-93/r7.speaker: ابن الأنباري
TABRISI:12:88-93/r7.claim: Jacob's letter identifies his lineage and recalls Abraham's rescue from the fire before narrating the family's trials.

TABRISI:12:88-93/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:88-93/r8.speaker: ابن عباس، الحسن
TABRISI:12:88-93/r8.claim: The letter says the brothers claimed Benjamin stole the king's measure, though Jacob insists his household does not steal.

TABRISI:12:90-92#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90-92#2/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:90-92#2/r1.claim: The brothers recognized Yusuf when his smile showed teeth like pearls, according to Ibn Abbas; another account says he removed his crown.

TABRISI:12:90-92#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90-92#2/r2.speaker: ابن الأنباري
TABRISI:12:90-92#2/r2.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says Yusuf's use of his own name rather than 'I am he' emphasizes that he is the brother whom they wronged and nearly killed.

TABRISI:12:90-92#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90-92#2/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:90-92#2/r3.claim: Yusuf calls Benjamin his brother as another wronged person like himself, and says God reunited them after a long separation.

TABRISI:12:90-92#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90-92#2/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:90-92#2/r4.claim: Whoever fears God and is patient through hardship and away from sin will receive the full reward of the good-doers.

TABRISI:12:90-92/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90-92/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:90-92/r1.claim: Izjāʾ means driving or moving something little by little; it can describe scraping by on small means or accepting a meagre, deficient amount.

TABRISI:12:90-92/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90-92/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:90-92/r2.claim: Qur'anic and poetic examples use izjāʾ for moving clouds and camels, and for a poor commodity accepted only by coaxing the buyer.

TABRISI:12:90-92/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90-92/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:90-92/r3.claim: Mann is a blessing; its root sense is cutting because a gift cuts the recipient off from poverty.

TABRISI:12:90-92/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90-92/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:90-92/r4.claim: Īthār is preferring one thing over another, related to choosing and selecting and rooted in giving priority to what leaves a good أثر.

TABRISI:12:90-92/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90-92/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:90-92/r5.claim: Khaṭaʾ is the opposite of correctness; the source gives its forms and cites a line by Imruʾ al-Qays.

TABRISI:12:90-92/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90-92/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:90-92/r7.claim: هل علمتم is a question intended to make the brothers acknowledge the matter; ما فعلتم is an object clause, and God's promise to reward the good is the conditional response.

TABRISI:12:90-92/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90-92/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:90-92/r8.claim: Calling them 'the good-doers' replaces a pronoun because fearing God and being patient are themselves forms of good action.

TABRISI:12:90/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90/r1.speaker: أبو جعفر، ابن كثير
TABRISI:12:90/r1.claim: Abu Jaʿfar and Ibn Kathir read the opening إن with kasra; several others use an unlengthened opening أن, while Abu ʿAmr, Qalun, and Zayd lengthen it, and the remainder use two hamzas.

TABRISI:12:90/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90/r2.speaker: أبي
TABRISI:12:90/r2.claim: A noncanonical reading attributed to Ubayy is أنك أو أنت يوسف; Ibn Jinni explains it as a hesitation followed by the clarification أنا يوسف.

TABRISI:12:90/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90/r3.speaker: ابن كثير
TABRISI:12:90/r3.claim: Ibn Kathir alone retains the yāʾ in من يتقي in both connected and paused reading; the other readers omit it.

TABRISI:12:90/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90/r4.speaker: أبو الحسن
TABRISI:12:90/r4.claim: Abu al-Hasan treats the open-hamza reading as an interrogative, parallel to asking whether God's favor is being claimed.

TABRISI:12:90/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90/r5.speaker: أبو علي
TABRISI:12:90/r5.claim: Abu ʿAli rejects a poetic analogy for dropping the yāʾ and instead treats من as a relative pronoun, 'the one who fears'; the following verb can coordinate by meaning because the construction resembles a conditional.

TABRISI:12:90/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:90/r6.claim: The grammatical coordination is compared to the reading فأصدق وأكن and to a jussive reading of ويذرهم in another verse.

TABRISI:12:90/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:90/r7.speaker: أبو الحسن
TABRISI:12:90/r7.claim: Abu al-Hasan heard رسلنا لديهم with a vowelless lām; this supports treating the final form as lightened in pronunciation.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r1.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو جعفر وابن محيصن
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r1.claim: These readers pronounce the opening as a declarative “Indeed, you are Joseph”; other readers articulate two hamzas, sometimes with an alif between.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r2.claim: One view says the brothers only compared Joseph to their brother rather than recognizing him.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r3.speaker: ابن إسحاق
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r3.claim: Ibn Ishaq says the brothers recognized Joseph.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r4.speaker: الضحاك عن ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r4.claim: They recognized him when he smiled and they saw teeth like Joseph's.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r5.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r5.claim: They recognized a mark on Joseph's temple, shared by Jacob, Isaac, and Sarah, when he removed his crown.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r6.speaker: ابن إسحاق
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r6.claim: Ibn Ishaq says Joseph lifted the veil, allowing them to recognize him.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r7.speaker: ابن الأنباري
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r7.claim: Joseph says “I am Joseph,” rather than “I am he,” to emphasize that he was the brother they had wronged and nearly killed.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r8.speaker: ابن الأنباري
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p280#2/r8.claim: Though the brothers knew Benjamin, “this is my brother” means this is the man wronged as I was.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r1.claim: “God favored us” may mean blessings in this world and the next, reunion after separation, or safety followed by honor.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r2.speaker: قنبل عن ابن كثير
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r2.claim: Qunbul retains the yāʾ in yattaqī in connected and paused reading; the other readers omit it in both.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r3.claim: Three interpretations attributed to Ibn Abbas are fearing illicit sex while bearing affliction, fearing it while enduring celibacy, or fearing God while bearing calamities.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r4.speaker: مجاهد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r4.claim: Mujahid says the person described avoids disobeying God and endures imprisonment.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r5.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p281/r5.claim: The promise means God does not waste the reward of anyone who has this character.

RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r1.claim: Grammatically, the lām is for emphasis, أنت is the subject, يوسف its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of إنّ.

RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r2.claim: Joseph names himself to emphasize the contrast between his brothers' extreme injustice and God's raising him to high rank; he similarly identifies his brother as another victim whom God favored.

RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says God favored Joseph and his brother with every kind of honor in this world and the next; others say the favor was their reunion.

RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r4.claim: The promise means whoever avoids God's disobedience and bears people's harm patiently will receive the reward of benefactors; the noun muḥsinīn encompasses the pious.

RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r5.claim: Joseph calls himself pious here; the claim that he committed sexual misconduct with the Aziz's wife would make his statement a lie in this solemn scene.

RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r6.speaker: ابن كثير
RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r6.claim: In the Qunbul transmission, Ibn Kathir retains the yāʾ in يتقي in both cases, treating من as a relative pronoun; ويصبر may then be nominative with its ending lightened.

RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p162#2/r7.claim: The other readers omit the yāʾ in يتق in both forms.

RAZI-FULL:v18p162/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p162/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p162/r6.claim: The readings of أإنك range from indicative to several interrogative forms, including Ubayy's أو أنت يوسف; the interrogative readings fit their recognition from Joseph's smile and pearl-like teeth, answered by أنا يوسف.

RAZI-FULL:v18p162/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p162/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v18p162/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas says the brothers recognized Joseph only when he removed his crown and they saw a birthmark in his hair like Jacob's and Isaac's.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r4.speaker: ابن إسحق
QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r4.claim: Ibn Isḥāq says the brothers humbled themselves by explaining their distress, Joseph felt compassion, disclosed his identity, and they asked whether he was really Joseph.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r5.claim: One report from Ibn ʿAbbās says Joseph smiled, his teeth looked like stringed pearls, and the brothers recognized him by resemblance.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r6.claim: A second report from Ibn ʿAbbās says they recognized Joseph only after he removed his crown, revealing a forehead mark like Jacob's; he raised the crown after asking what they had done.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās relates Jacob's letter recounting the trials of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and saying he had neither stolen nor fathered a thief; Joseph trembled, wept, and revealed himself.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r8.speaker: ابن كثير
QURTUBI-FULL:12:89-90/r8.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads innaka as a declarative, though the reading may also be interrogative, as in the cited example from 26:26.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r1.claim: I am Joseph means I am the one wronged and intended for killing; Joseph does not say I am he, magnifying the story.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r2.claim: God's favor upon Joseph and his brother means their deliverance and kingship.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r3.claim: Taqwā means fearing God, while patience means enduring trials and abstaining from sins; God rewards those who patiently endure and obey.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r4.speaker: ابن كثير
QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r4.claim: Ibn Kathīr retains the yāʾ in yattaqī; this is valid if man is a relative pronoun, with yattaqī in its clause and wa-yaṣbir nominative.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r5.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r5.claim: The retained yāʾ may also be read conditionally, with yattaqī jussive by deletion of its original final ḍamma and wa-yaṣbir either jussive or nominative.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:90-92/r6.claim: The majority reading is plain; the hāʾ in innahu refers to the matter being discussed, and the clause is its predicate.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r1.claim: The question is confirmatory, marked by inna and the emphatic lām; Ibn Kathir instead reads it as a straightforward assertion.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r2.speaker: ابن كثير
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r2.claim: Ibn Kathir reads the brothers' words as an assertion rather than a confirmatory question.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r3.speaker: قيل
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r3.claim: One explanation is that the brothers recognized Joseph from his appearance and bearing when he spoke.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r4.speaker: قيل
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r4.claim: Another explanation is that his smile revealed his distinctive teeth.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r5.speaker: قيل
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r5.claim: A third explanation says that removing his crown exposed a white birthmark like Sarah's and Jacob's.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r6.claim: Joseph identifies Benjamin as his full brother to distinguish himself and honor him by including him in God's favor upon them.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r7.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r7.claim: Piety means fearing God; patience can mean enduring trials, performing obedience, or avoiding sins.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:90/r8.claim: Calling the patient and God-fearing brothers benefactors highlights that beneficence combines both qualities.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r1.speaker: الكوفي والشامي
NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r1.claim: The Kufi and Shami readings use two hamzas in the question 'Are you indeed Joseph?'

NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r2.claim: The lām is an initiating lām; anta is the subject and Yūsuf its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of inna.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r3.claim: Joseph mentions his brother in answering their question about his identity because it clarifies the answer.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r4.claim: He acknowledges God's favor in restoring family after separation and mentions safety and honor without reproach.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r5.claim: Taqwā means avoiding obscenity and patience means refraining from sin and persevering in obedience; al-muḥsinīn replaces a pronoun because it encompasses both traits.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p203#2/r6.claim: Alternatively, the one who fears his Lord and patiently bears affliction will receive reward in this world and the next.

QASHANI:12:84-92/r7.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:84-92/r7.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:84-92/r7.claim: Joseph's question about what they did to him and his brother signals the heart's descent to the chest so the powers recognize it and recall their former ignorance; their recognition expresses wonder at its luminous majesty.

QASHANI:12:84-92/r8.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:84-92/r8.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:84-92/r8.claim: The brothers' admission that God favored Joseph guides disciplined faculties to recognize their incompletion; no reproach reflects their natural constitution, and forgiveness signifies purification through virtue and obedience.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p319/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p319/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p319/r5.claim: The brothers recognized that the speaker knew their history; one report says he lifted the screen and crown, revealing the family mark and his identity.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p319/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p319/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p319/r6.claim: Another view calls their question confirmation because they already knew him by signs mentioned earlier.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p319/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p319/r7.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p319/r7.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says his appearance and manner of speech revealed him as a Muslim descendant of Abraham rather than an Egyptian notable.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320#2/r1.speaker: قنبل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320#2/r1.claim: For Qunbul’s yatqī, the author prefers a jussive with deleted final yāʾ on a rare but reported dialect, rejecting Abu Ali’s restriction to poetry.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320#2/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320#2/r2.claim: Al-muḥsinīn may be general or replace a pronoun because it encompasses the pious and patient; the meaning is that their reward is not lost.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r1.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r1.claim: Most readers pronounce the question with an interrogative hamza; readings differ in how the two hamzas are realized or softened.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r10.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r10.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes it as fearing God and punishment, refraining from sins, and persevering in obedience.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r11.claim: Other glosses tie piety and patience to calamities or people’s harm; the author says these are specifications drawn from Joseph’s circumstances.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r2.speaker: قتادة وابن محيصن وابن كثير
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r2.claim: Qatada, Ibn Muhaysin, and Ibn Kathir read innaka without the interrogative hamza, which is apparently understood rather than a plain assertion.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r3.speaker: أبي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r3.claim: Ubayy has a reading adding ‘or are you Joseph?’; grammarians supply a deleted predicate or repeat the name, which al-Zamakhshari takes as startled insistence.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r4.speaker: أبي بن كعب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r4.claim: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb’s reading asks, ‘or are you Joseph?’

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r5.claim: In the common reading, the emphatic lām may mark separation before the predicate or appear with anta as subject; anta cannot be emphatic because the lām intervenes.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r6.claim: Joseph identifies Benjamin because the earlier question mentioned them together, then credits God with their reunion and comfort after estrangement.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r7.claim: The author prefers taking piety and patience generally, rather than restricting them to Joseph’s ordeals.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r8.speaker: مجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r8.claim: Mujahid interprets piety as leaving sin and patience as enduring prison.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r9.speaker: النخعي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p320/r9.claim: Al-Nakhaʿi interprets the pair as avoiding adultery and bearing celibacy.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r1.claim: Qunbul retains the final ياء of يتقي in pause and liaison; other readers delete it, as expected for a jussive.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r10.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r10.claim: The conditional result is linked through the generality of المحسنين, an omitted منهم, or أل replacing that pronoun.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r2.claim: The strongest account is a dialect retaining weak letters in this environment; poetic evidence includes Qays ibn Zuhayr and two other verses.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r3.speaker: سيبويه
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r3.claim: Sibawayh says the jussive deletes the underlying vowel; the weak letter follows its deletion to distinguish moods.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r4.claim: An objection says the jussive marker already distinguishes mood; the reply is that retained ياء can make زرني أعطيك ambiguous.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r5.speaker: ابن السراج
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r5.claim: Ibn al-Sarraj instead says the jussive directly affects and deletes the weak letter.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r6.claim: A second account treats من as relative and يتق as indicative; it is challenged by the jussive ويصبر.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r7.claim: The jussive ويصبر is explained by successive vowels, with Abu Amr's readings at 3:160 and 2:67 as parallels.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r8.claim: Other replies invoke resemblance between relative and conditional من, treatment as pause, or conditional-like semantics; the author prefers “resemblance” to “supposition.”

SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#2/r9.claim: The author allows a reverse account—conditional من keeps ياء by resemblance to relative من—but finds it odd that a distant العامل affects يتق and not nearby ويصبر.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#3/r1.claim: The result clause is linked to its condition through the general sense of المحسنين.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#3/r2.claim: A second link supplies المحسنين منهم, “the good-doers among them.”

SAMIN-DURR:12:90#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90#3/r3.claim: A third link treats أل as standing for the omitted possessive pronoun; the underlying phrase is محسنيهم.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r1.claim: Ibn Kathir reads إنك with one hamza; the other readers use two hamzas as an interrogative, with known easing differences.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r2.claim: The single-hamza reading may be declarative, though that is unlikely with one speaker; the reports can be reconciled by assigning question and statement to different brothers.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r3.claim: Alternatively, its interrogative particle is omitted, supplied by context and the other reading.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r4.claim: In لأنت يوسف, أنت can be a subject with يوسف as predicate, making the clause خبر إن under an initial lām.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r5.claim: Alternatively, أنت is a pronoun of separation; it cannot be emphasis because this lām does not precede emphasis.

SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r6.speaker: أبو الفتح
SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r6.claim: Ubayy's أإنك أو أنت يوسف may omit إن's predicate: “Are you not Joseph, or are you Joseph?”

SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r7.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:12:90/r7.claim: Al-Zamakhshari understands the omitted first alternative as إنك يوسف, repeated as an astonished request for confirmation.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r1.claim: Hearing of his brothers' hardship and his father's grief moved Yusuf to compassion and tears; a report says he lifted his crown to reveal a mark on his forehead before identifying himself.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r3.claim: Yusuf revealed himself with God's permission, just as he had concealed his identity from them earlier by God's command; God relieved the hardship, as in the promise of ease with hardship.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r4.speaker: أبي بن كعب
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r4.claim: Ubayy ibn Ka'b read the brothers' question as 'or are you Yusuf?'.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r5.speaker: ابن محيصن
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r5.claim: Ibn Muhaysin read the question without the initial interrogative hamza: 'you are indeed Yusuf'.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r6.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r6.claim: The common interrogative reading is preferred because it conveys the brothers' astonishment at recognizing Yusuf after repeated visits while he knew them and concealed himself.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r7.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p408/r7.claim: Yusuf says God favored the brothers by reuniting them after separation; the brothers admit his superiority in character, appearance, power, rule, and—according to those who deny that they were prophets—prophethood, and confess their wrongdoing.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r3.claim: The brothers suspect his identity and ask emphatically whether he is Joseph; the author says the exchange was apparently without an interpreter.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r4.claim: Joseph identifies himself and Benjamin as brothers, then says God has favored them by reuniting them in a good state.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r5.claim: Qunbul retains the final yāʾ of yattaqi in both forms, treating the verb like a sound verb to signify complete, constant piety.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r6.claim: Taqwā means warding off harm by following guidance, and patience means restraining the self while enduring the bitterness of denied desire.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p93/r7.claim: Joseph reveals himself gradually to avert panic, prevent renewed treachery, and let the brothers recognize his justice and forgiveness before bringing Jacob to Egypt.

DURR-FULL:v4p577/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p577/r1.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v4p577/r1.claim: The brothers recognized that the man belonged to their family, then realized he was Joseph, son of Jacob.

DURR-FULL:v4p577/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p577/r2.speaker: الأعمش
DURR-FULL:v4p577/r2.claim: Al-Aʿmash reports that Yahya ibn Waththab read the question with one hamza.

DURR-FULL:v4p577/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p577/r3.speaker: الضحاك
DURR-FULL:v4p577/r3.claim: Al-Dahhak says Abdullah's reading adds that Joseph and Benjamin were kin to one another.

DURR-FULL:v4p577/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p577/r4.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v4p577/r4.claim: One gloss takes fearing God as avoiding adultery and patience as remaining chaste; God does not waste the righteous person's reward.

DURR-FULL:v4p577/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p577/r5.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
DURR-FULL:v4p577/r5.claim: A report from earlier scripture says envy harms the envier, while the envied person is saved by patience.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r1.claim: The brothers' question is a confirmation-seeking expression of astonishment, hence emphatic إن and lām despite its interrogative form; Ibn Kathir, Qatada, and Ibn Muhaysin read without the interrogative hamza, apparently still implying a question.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r10.speaker: أبو البقاء
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r10.claim: Abu al-Baqa treats قد من الله علينا as a new independent sentence; another parses it as a circumstantial clause, but Al-Alusi finds that difficult because هذا points to one person while علينا refers to both and the needed governor is absent.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r2.speaker: ابن كثير وقتادة وابن محيصن
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r2.claim: Ibn Kathir, Qatada, and Ibn Muhaysin read إنك without the interrogative hamza; al-Bahr finds a question still implied, while a plain assertion is unlikely unless different speakers' words were combined.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r3.speaker: أبي
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r3.claim: Ubayy's reading adds أو: 'Are you ... or are you Joseph?' Ibn Jinni and al-Zamakhshari supply an omitted predicate in different ways; al-Kashf prefers the lower-ellipsis version, while al-Tibi suggests the brothers contrast his known status with Joseph's identity.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r4.claim: In either main reading, أنت is the subject and يوسف its predicate, with their clause serving as the predicate of إن; أنت cannot emphasize إن's pronoun because the lām intervenes.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r5.claim: Suggested ways the brothers recognized Joseph include his features and bearing, seeing him after he drew them near, hearing him after a curtain was raised, recognizing his pearl-like shining teeth when he smiled, or seeing a birthmark shared with Jacob, Isaac, and Sarah; his speech also sounded Abrahamic and Muslim.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r6.claim: Some say they only guessed and did not recognize him until he identified himself; Al-Alusi says the earlier recognition explanations are the relied-upon view.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r7.claim: Joseph answers directly, then calls the second man his brother from both parents to further establish his identity; one reading treats this as a wise redirection to God's favor, while another sees it as completing the answer about what befell Joseph and his brother.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r8.speaker: الإرشاد
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r8.claim: Irshad reads 'God has favored us' as rescue from trial, reunion after separation, honor after humiliation, and intimacy after estrangement, completing the brothers' earlier question about what they did to Joseph and his brother.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r9.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v13p48/r9.claim: One explanation sees Joseph's mention of his brother as an answer to their demand that Benjamin be returned: Benjamin is Joseph's brother, not theirs, so they have no claim to him.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r1.claim: The pronoun in 'God does not waste their reward' refers to the doers of good; using the explicit noun instead of a pronoun signals that people of taqwa and patience are also people of ihsan, and the sentence gives the reason for God's favor.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r2.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r2.claim: Abu Hayyan declines to restrict taqwa and patience to a single form of conduct.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r3.speaker: مجاهد
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r3.claim: Mujahid interprets taqwa as refraining from sin and patience as enduring prison.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r4.speaker: النخعي
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r4.claim: Al-Nakha'i interprets taqwa as avoiding adultery and patience as enduring celibacy.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r5.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r5.claim: Another interpretation is avoiding sins and bearing people's harm.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r6.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes the qualities as fearing God, refraining from sins, and persevering in both duties and avoiding prohibitions; al-Fara'id objects that taqwa can keep its literal sense of guarding against neglected commands and forbidden acts.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r7.speaker: الفرائد
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r7.claim: Al-Fara'id says taqwa should retain its literal meaning of avoiding omissions of duties and violations, while patience concerns involuntary hardships; patience may be the specific after the general or mean remaining steadfast in taqwa.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r8.speaker: الطيبي
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r8.claim: Al-Tibi reads the statement as rebuking Joseph's brothers for not fearing God or patiently obeying God and their father; an objection says the other interpretation conveys the same admonition, which Al-Alusi questions.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r9.speaker: قنبل
ALUSI-FULL:v13p49/r9.claim: Qunbul reads يتقي with an extra yā; grammarians propose an emphatic yā with jussive, deletion of an estimated vowel, a nominative relative reading, or a silent final rā in يصبر. Al-Bahr prefers the rare dialectal jussive, also attested in prose despite Abu Ali's restriction to poetry.

ELMALILI:12:89-93/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:12:89-93/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:12:89-93/r2.claim: Yusuf's words strike the brothers suddenly, and they infer in astonishment that the speaker is Yusuf before asking him directly.

ELMALILI:12:89-93/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:12:89-93/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:12:89-93/r3.claim: Yusuf identifies himself and his brother, who is beside him in a position of honor and had seemed to escape their notice.

ELMALILI:12:89-93/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:12:89-93/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:12:89-93/r4.claim: To avoid sounding proud, Yusuf gives thanks to God and teaches that God does not waste the reward of those who fear Him and remain patient.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r1.claim: The passage dates Egypt's second kingdom to the Hyksos, also called Amalekites or shepherds and identified here as Arabs; their division lasted 511 years, 2214–1703 BCE.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r2.claim: The brothers recognized Yusuf from his speech, appearance, and their father's hint in Q 12:86, understanding the allusion to Yusuf himself.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r3.claim: إن, the initial lām, and the separative pronoun emphasize how certain they were that he was Yusuf.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r4.claim: The confirmatory question seeks Yusuf's ratification because they already know his identity.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r5.speaker: ابن كثير
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p48/r5.claim: Ibn Kathir reads إنك without a question as a declarative recognition (“we know you”); this pragmatic meaning explains why Yusuf's answer needs no emphasis.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r1.claim: “This is my brother” expresses wonder at God's reunion of the brothers after a long separation; “God has favored us” spells out the point.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r2.claim: Yusuf explains God's favor through piety and patience: he and Benjamin remained pious and patient, implicitly reminding the brothers that they had failed in both respects toward them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r3.claim: Yusuf uses an emotionally charged moment and visible proof of his sincerity to teach how to seek divine favor, a rhetorical opportunity for admonition.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r4.claim: “The people of excellence” replaces a pronoun to identify this as excellence and generalize the promise, including Yusuf and Benjamin.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r5.claim: The Prophet's statement “I am the most God-fearing of you and know God best” illustrates that prophets may speak of their own virtue when conveying a lesson.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r6.claim: The brothers' oath expresses their recognition that Yusuf's worldly blessings were God's preference for him, not information he lacked.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r7.claim: The brothers' admission of being mistaken means they committed a crime; Yusuf responds by removing blame and reproach from them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p49/r8.claim: لا تثريب عليكم is a concise idiom whose sentence ends at عليكم, like لا بأس; compare Q 75:11.

TABATABAI:12:89-92/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:89-92/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:89-92/r2.claim: The brothers’ emphatic question seeks an admission after signs established Joseph’s identity, rather than expressing real uncertainty.

TABATABAI:12:89-92/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:89-92/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:89-92/r3.claim: Joseph adds that Benjamin is his brother though they did not ask, because God favored both brothers, who had both been objects of envy.

TABATABAI:12:89-92/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:89-92/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:89-92/r4.claim: Joseph explains God’s favor through outward causes and invites his brothers to beneficence, which is realized through piety and patience.

ASAD-NOTES:12:89#n92/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:89#n92/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:89#n92/r1.claim: The phrase literally begins whoever is.

ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.claim: Unlike Genesis' romantic account of Joseph's fortunes, the Qur'anic story illustrates God's unfathomable direction of human affairs: people may hate what is good for them or love what is bad for them.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The ending summarizes that God does not waste the reward of those who fear Him and remain steadfast; the episode corroborates the historical testimony in Hūd.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Joseph used his brothers' ignorance to test whether they had changed; eventually they recognized his identity and he called his parents and brothers to join him.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The brothers likely suspected Joseph from his appearance and manner but could not believe a boy cast into a Canaanite well could become Egypt's ruler; those fixed on appearances miss God's power.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Joseph's reply is the anecdote's central essence and forms the sūrah's theme.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Iḥsān, understood as thoroughness, is a prerequisite for accepted God-consciousness and steadfastness: worship with awareness that God sees you, even when you do not see Him.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r1.claim: Joseph identifies himself by recalling what his brothers did to him and Benjamin, fulfilling the revelation that he would later tell them of it when they did not recognize him (12:15).

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r2.claim: His brothers admit their wrong and apologize, and Joseph tells them he forgives them.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r3.claim: Envy cannot block a blessing God has decreed; the Prophet prayed that no one can withhold what God gives, and the brothers ultimately acknowledge God favored Joseph over them.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r4.speaker: Resûlullah
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r4.claim: The Prophet’s prayer says no one can prevent what God grants, and no one can grant what God withholds.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r5.speaker: Ziyâ Paşa
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:89/r5.claim: Ziya Pasha’s couplet says divine power eventually makes tyrants admit that God favored another over them.

QIRAAT-ER:12:90:18#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:12:90:18#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:12:90:18#1/r1.claim: The full indicative rather than apocopated jussive form shifts man from a conditional particle to a relative pronoun.

QIRAAT-ER:12:90:2#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:12:90:2#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:12:90:2#1/r1.claim: Dropping interrogative hamza changes the utterance from a question to an assertion.

STUDYQURAN:12:89/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:89/r4.speaker: Bḍ
STUDYQURAN:12:89/r4.claim: One report says the brothers recognized Joseph when he spoke these words, or when he smiled.

STUDYQURAN:12:89/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:89/r5.speaker: Sh
STUDYQURAN:12:89/r5.claim: Another report says the brothers recognized Joseph when he removed his crown.

STUDYQURAN:12:89/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:89/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:12:89/r6.claim: The statement that God does not neglect the virtuous’ reward is linked to 9:120, 11:11, 11:115, and 12:56.
